instructions: Slice the peppers into thin strips, discarding the stems and seeds. Slice the onion into thin strips. Mince the garlic.
Pat the pork dry. Mix the flour, 3/4 tsp of the salt and the black pepper on a plate. Lightly press each chop into it.

Heat 2 tbsp of the olive oil in a large, wide skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add half the pork in a single layer. Cook for 1 1/2 minutes on each side, until golden. Transfer to a plate. Repeat with the other half.
Add the last 2 tbsp of oil, the peppers, the onion and 1/4 tsp of the salt to the same pan. Cook over medium-high heat for 5 minutes, stirring often, until the peppers are soft and browned in spots.
Add the garlic and the paprika. Cook for 30 seconds, stirring.
Add the crushed tomatoes and the chicken stock. Scrape up the browned bits from the bottom of the pan. Simmer for 4 minutes, until the sauce is thick enough to coat a spoon.

Return the pork and any juices from the plate to the pan, and spoon the sauce over it. Cover and cook over low heat for 4 minutes. You're cooking it to 145°F in the middle, so if you have a thermometer, check it there. No thermometer? Cut into the thickest chop: it should be just barely pink.
Taste it. If it's flat, add a pinch more salt.
method_notes: No version of this dish had a rating, so this is a fallback with Publico's lomo con pimientos as the lead. It floured and seared the pork, built a sauce of onion, garlic, paprika and tomato, and cooked the pork in it with the peppers for about 20 minutes. It uses roasted red or piquillo peppers; the dish was named for sweet green peppers, so this version fries Cubanelle peppers, as Directo al Paladar does for its green-pepper lomo. To make it fit 30 minutes the pork is cut thin and simmers for 4 minutes, not 20. Total time is 30 minutes.
